Tim Duncan was born on April 25, 1976.
Timothy Theodore Duncan is his full name.
Duncan is an American former professional basketball player.
Duncan spent his entire 19-year career with the San Antonio Spurs.
Duncan's nickname is "the Big Fundamental".
Duncan is widely regarded as the greatest power forward of all time and one of the greatest players in NBA history.
Duncan was a central contributor to the franchise's success during the 2000s and 2010s.
Duncan was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2020.
Duncan was named to the NBA 75th Anniversary Team in 2021.
Duncan was born and raised on Saint Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands.
Duncan's parents are Ione, a professional midwife from Anguilla, and William Duncan, a mason.
Duncan has two older sisters named Cheryl and Tricia.
Duncan has an older brother named Scott who became a film director and cinematographer.
Cheryl was a champion swimmer before becoming a nurse.
Tricia swam for the U.S. Virgin Islands at the 1988 Summer Olympics in Seoul.
Duncan initially aspired to be a competitive swimmer but took up basketball at age 14 after Hurricane Hugo destroyed the island's only Olympic-sized pool.
Hurricane Hugo destroyed the island's only Olympic-sized swimming pool, forcing Duncan to swim in the ocean instead.
Duncan's fear of sharks ruined his enthusiasm for swimming competitively again.
Duncan's mother died on April 24, 1990, the day before his 14th birthday.
On her deathbed, Duncan's mother made him and his sisters promise to graduate from college.
Duncan was forced to swim in the ocean instead of using the island's Olympic-sized pool after Hurricane Hugo destroyed it.
Duncan never swam competitively again after Hurricane Hugo.
Duncan's brother-in-law inspired him to turn to basketball when he had difficulties adapting to the game initially.
Duncan overcame his awkwardness and became a standout player for St. Dunstan's Episcopal High School, averaging 25 points per game as a senior.
Wake Forest University basketball coach Dave Odom was interested in Duncan after the 16-year-old played NBA star Alonzo Mourning to a draw in a pick-up game.
Duncan joined Wake Forest Demon Deacons despite scholarship offers from other universities.
The Demon Deacons had reached the Sweet 16 before losing leading scorer Rodney Rogers, who entered the 1993 NBA draft.
Coach Dave Odom considered redshirting Duncan but was forced to play him after fellow freshman Makhtar N'Diaye violated NCAA rules and transferred to Michigan.
Duncan struggled with early transition problems and was scoreless in his first college game.
As the year progressed, Duncan and teammate Randolph Childress led the Deacons to a 20–11 win–loss record.
Duncan's style of play combined low-post moves, mid-range bank shots, and tough defense.
Duncan was chosen to represent the U.S. in the 1994 Goodwill Games.
Duncan worked towards a degree in psychology while taking classes in anthropology and Chinese literature.
Duncan was one of Coach Dave Odom's more intellectual students despite his height.
Duncan established his reputation as a stoic player, earning the nickname "Mr. Spock".
In the 1994–95 NCAA season, Duncan led the Demon Deacons into the Atlantic Coast Conference (ACC) championship game against North Carolina.
During that game, Duncan neutralized Rasheed Wallace while Childress sealed the win with a jump shot in overtime.
Duncan's season averages of 16.8 points and 12.5 rebounds per game earned him ACC Defensive Player of the Year award.
Duncan was named All-ACC First Team for his performance that year.
Duncan became the third-best shot-blocker in NCAA history with 3.98 blocks per game during the 1994–95 season.
In the 1995–96 NCAA season, Duncan led the Demon Deacons to a 26–6 record overall and an ACC championship.
Duncan's season averages of 19.1 points and 12.3 rebounds per game earned him another ACC Defensive Player of the Year award.
Duncan was named ACC Player of the Year for his performance that year.
Duncan stayed in college for a full four years despite being one of the best prospects among those eligible for the NBA.
Duncan led Wake Forest to their first 13 games with Loren Woods easing pressure close to the basket.
The 1996–97 team won their first ACC title, but failed to win a third consecutive title due to a slump in performance.
In January 12, 1997, Duncan scored 26 points and 14 rebounds against Duke.
On January 24, 1997, Duncan scored 16 points, 15 rebounds, and 5 blocks against Clemson.
During the NCAA tournament, Stanford University eliminated Wake Forest with a 72–66 win.
Duncan finished his college career as the all-time leading rebounder in NCAA history (post-1973 era).
Duncan left college as the all-time leading shot-blocker in ACC history with 481 blocks.
In college, Duncan co-authored a chapter on aversive interpersonal behaviors with Mark Leary.
Duncan entered the 1997 NBA draft after earning his degree in psychology.
The San Antonio Spurs drafted Duncan with the first pick in the 1997 NBA draft.
The Spurs were coming off an injury-riddled 1996–97 season when they drafted Duncan.
David Robinson, the Spurs' best player, was sidelined for most of the 1996–97 season.
In his rookie season, Duncan started in all 82 regular-season games and averaged 21.1 points, 11.9 rebounds, 2.7 assists, and 2.5 blocks per game.
Duncan earned All-NBA First Team honors for his performance as a rookie.
Duncan was chosen to the 1998 NBA All-Star Game by coaches in his rookie season.
In his first playoff game against the Phoenix Suns, Duncan had a bad first half but finished with 32 points and 10 rebounds.
The Spurs defeated the Phoenix Suns 3–1 in their first-round playoff series.
Duncan was named NBA Rookie of the Month every single month during his rookie season.
Duncan's mental toughness impressed Spurs coach Gregg Popovich, who praised Duncan's "demeanor" as remarkable.
In Game 2 against Houston Rockets, Charles Barkley said, "I have seen the future and he wears number 21."
The Spurs qualified for the 1998 NBA playoffs as the fifth seed but lost in the second round to Utah Jazz.
During the lockout-shortened 1998–99 season, Duncan averaged 21.7 points, 11.4 rebounds, 2.4 assists, and 2.5 blocks per game.
The Spurs started with a lackluster 6–8 record in the 1998–99 season but finished with a 31–5 run.
Duncan was voted to the NBA All-Defensive Second Team for his defensive contributions as a rookie.
In the 1999 NBA playoffs, the Spurs defeated Minnesota Timberwolves 3–1, swept Los Angeles Lakers and Portland Trail Blazers 4–0, and defeated New York Knicks 4–1 in the Finals.
Duncan was named NBA Finals MVP after leading the Spurs to their first-ever NBA championship.
In Game 5 of the 1999 NBA Finals, Duncan scored 28 points and 18 rebounds as the Spurs protected a lead with the ball in the Knicks' possession.
The Spurs defeated the Phoenix Suns in the second round of the 1999 playoffs but lost to Utah Jazz in the Western Conference finals.
In the 1999–2000 season, Duncan averaged 23.2 points and 12.4 rebounds per game.
Duncan was named to both All-NBA and All-Defensive First Teams for his performance that year.
The Spurs were eliminated from the 2000 NBA playoffs in the first round by Phoenix Suns.
In the 2000–01 season, Duncan averaged 22.2 points, 12.2 rebounds, 3.0 assists, and 2.3 blocks per game.
Duncan was again named to both All-NBA and All-Defensive First Teams for his performance that year.
In the 2001 NBA playoffs, the Spurs were defeated by the Lakers in four straight games despite Duncan's strong play.
In the 2001–02 season, Duncan improved statistically with career highs in scoring (25.5 points per game) and rebounding (12.7 boards per game).
Duncan was named NBA Most Valuable Player for his performance that year.
David Robinson announced he would retire after the 2001–02 season due to aging.
In the 2002–03 season, Duncan averaged career highs in scoring and rebounding.
Duncan led the Spurs into the Western Conference Semifinals against the Lakers but was defeated 4–1 by the eventual champions.
On July 16, 2003, Duncan signed a seven-year, $122 million contract with the Spurs.
Before the 2003–04 season began, the Spurs lost their captain David Robinson to retirement.
Duncan led a reformed Spurs team that included Rasho Nesterović, Bruce Bowen, Manu Ginóbili, and Tony Parker as key players.
In the 2003–04 season, Duncan averaged 22.3 points, 12.4 rebounds, 3.1 assists, and 2.7 blocks per game.
The Spurs won the second seed for the 2005 NBA playoffs with a 60–22 record in the regular season.
In the first round of the 2005 NBA playoffs, the Spurs defeated Denver Nuggets four games to one.
In the semi-finals against Seattle SuperSonics, Duncan led his team to two decisive victories after splitting the first four games.
The Spurs defeated Phoenix Suns 4–1 and earned a spot in the 2005 NBA Finals against Detroit Pistons.
Duncan was pitted against Ben Wallace's defensively strong frontcourt during the 2005 NBA Finals.
In Game 7 of the 2005 NBA Finals, Duncan recorded 25 points and 11 rebounds as the Spurs defeated the Pistons.
Duncan won his third NBA Finals MVP Award in 2005.
Duncan suffered from plantar fasciitis for most of the 2005–06 season, which affected his output.
In the 2006 NBA playoffs against Dallas Mavericks, Duncan outscored Dirk Nowitzki 32.2 to 27.1 points but fouled out in overtime.
Duncan was named as a Western Conference starter for the 2007 NBA All-Star Game.
The Spurs defeated Denver Nuggets 4–1 in the first round of the 2007 NBA playoffs.
In the second round, the Spurs defeated Phoenix Suns 4–2 and advanced to the Western Conference Finals against Utah Jazz.
Duncan led the Spurs to a 4–1 series win over Utah Jazz in the Western Conference Finals.
The Spurs swept Cleveland Cavaliers 4–0 in the 2007 NBA Finals, earning Duncan his fourth championship.
Duncan was named NBA Finals MVP for his performance in the 2007 NBA Finals.
Duncan was diagnosed with chronic knee tendinosis during the 2008–09 season.
The Spurs qualified for the playoffs as the third seed with a 54–28 record in the regular season.
In the first round of the 2009 NBA playoffs, the Spurs defeated Dallas 4–2 but were eliminated by Phoenix in the next round.
Duncan became the Spurs' all-time leader in points scored and games played during the 2010–11 season.
The Spurs compiled a 13-game winning streak to go 13–2 after 15 games in the 2010–11 season.
On November 30, 2010, Duncan recorded his third career triple-double against Golden State Warriors.
On December 2, 2013, Duncan became the oldest player to record a 20–20 game in NBA history.
The Spurs finished the 2013–14 regular season with a league-best 62 wins.
In the 2014 NBA playoffs, the Spurs swept Los Angeles Lakers and Golden State before defeating Oklahoma City in six games.
Duncan recorded his 500th playoff block against Oklahoma City, becoming the first player to reach that milestone.
The Spurs met Miami Heat in the 2014 NBA Finals but lost the series 4–1.
On June 28, 2016, Duncan's 21 jersey was retired by the San Antonio Spurs.
Duncan announced his retirement from the NBA after 19 seasons with San Antonio on July 11, 2016.
In September 2016, Gregg Popovich indicated that Duncan would have a coaching role with the team in the 2016–17 season.
On December 18, 2016, the Spurs retired Duncan's No. 21 jersey during a postgame ceremony.
Duncan was selected as one of the last two players for the United States national team for the 1998 World Basketball Championship but did not participate due to an NBA lockout.
In 1999, Duncan played in the Olympic Qualifying Team and averaged 12.7 points, 9.1 rebounds, and 2.4 blocks per game.
Duncan's participation in the 2003 USA team was later replaced with CBA and college players due to an NBA lockout.
In 2004, Duncan played for the USA team that qualified for the 2004 Summer Olympics but missed the tournament due to a knee injury.
Duncan has gained a reputation as a clutch player, evidenced by his three NBA Finals MVP awards.
Duncan's playoff career averages are higher than his regular season statistics.
Bill Russell praised Duncan on his passing ability and rated him as one of the most efficient players of his generation.
Kareem Abdul-Jabbar shared this view, considering Duncan to be one of the greatest power forwards in NBA history.
Duncan is considered "boring" by some due to his simple but effective style of play.
Duncan stated that he likes his bank shot because it feels good and is easy for him.
Duncan's close relationship with Gregg Popovich has been described as "the greatest love story in sports."
Duncan received a number of individual honors, including being named MVP twice (2002, 2003), five-time NBA champion (1999, 2003, 2005, 2007, 2014), and three-time NBA Finals MVP (1999, 2003, 2005).
Duncan was named to the ACC 50th Anniversary men's basketball team in 2002.
In his debut year in the NBA (1998), Duncan was voted Rookie of the Year and elected into the All-Rookie Team.
Duncan has been named to 15 NBA All-Star teams, 15 All-NBA Teams, and 15 All-Defensive Teams.
Duncan is one of only four players to receive All-NBA First Team honors in each of his first eight seasons (1998–2005).
Duncan is the only player in NBA history to receive All-NBA and All-Defensive honors in his first 13 seasons (1997–2010).
Duncan was named by the Association for Professional Basketball Research as one of the "100 Greatest Professional Basketball Players of the 20th Century."
In the 2001–02 season, Duncan won the IBM Player Award and the Sporting News MVP Award.
On February 18, 2006, Duncan was named one of the Next 10 Greatest Players on the tenth anniversary of the release of the NBA's 50th Anniversary All-Time Team by TNT broadcasting crew.
In 2009, Duncan was ranked 8th by Slam magazine in their list of the top 50 NBA players of all time.
Sports Illustrated named Duncan its NBA Player of the Decade.
In 2022, The Athletic ranked Duncan as the ninth greatest player in NBA history.
Duncan was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame on August 29, 2020.
Duncan was named to the NBA 75th Anniversary Team in 2021.
On November 12, 2020, Duncan stepped down as assistant coach of the Spurs.
Duncan married Amy Sherrill in July 2001 and had two children before their divorce in August 2013.
In 2017, Duncan welcomed his first child with a new girlfriend.

Duncan established the Tim Duncan Foundation to fund programs involving health awareness and research, education, and youth sports and recreation in San Antonio, Winston-Salem, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
The foundation's major events have included the Tim Duncan Bowling for Dollar$ Charity Bowl-A-Thon and the Slam Duncan Charity Golf Classic.
Between 2001 and 2002, the foundation raised more than $350,000 for breast and prostate cancer research.
Duncan has supported various organizations such as the Children's Bereavement Center, the Children's Center of San Antonio, and the Cancer Therapy and Research Center.
In August 2017, BlackJack Speed Shop organized urgently needed supplies for Hurricane Harvey victims in partnership with The Tim Duncan Foundation.
Duncan cites his late mother as his main inspiration and adopted her nursery rhyme "Good, Better, Best" as his personal motto.
On and off the court, Duncan believes that dedication, teamwork, and camaraderie are the three most important values.
Duncan chose No. 21 for his jersey because it was his brother-in-law's college number, which inspired him in basketball.
Duncan cites Hall-of-Fame Los Angeles Lakers point guard Magic Johnson as his childhood idol.
Duncan was honored with the Virgin Islands Medal of Honor, the highest award bestowed by the Virgin Islands territorial government.
Duncan has been celebrated in several "Tim Duncan Day" ceremonies.
Duncan enjoys Renaissance fairs and the fantasy role-playing game Dungeons & Dragons.
In 2015, Duncan sued his former investment adviser for over $20 million in losses.
In March 2020, Duncan offered to pay for airline tickets for college students in the U.S. Virgin Islands to travel home during the COVID-19 pandemic.
